text: The assembly will now hear an address by
his excellency
David Ranibbuk Adyang,
president of and head of state of the
Republic of Nairo.
I request protocol to escort his
excellency and invite him to address the
assembly.
Mr. President,
Mr. Secretary General, excellencies,
distinguished delegates,
I bring you warm greetings from my
people and my country.
We meet under the theme restoring trust,
managing transformation.
A United Nations that delivers for all.
For my country, that means ensuring no
nation, regardless of size or distance,
is left behind as the world changes
around us.
Mr. President, let me begin by
congratulating you on your election to
preside over this 81st session.
My delegation assures you of our full
support and we thank your predecessor
for the stewardship of the 80th session.
We also pay tribute to Secretary General
Antonio Gutz.
This is the last general debate of his
tenure and my country records his
gratitude for a decade in which the
smaller states were heard more often
than before.
I have traveled far to speak on matters
that may seem distinct but are united by
a single fundamental principle.
The right of every people to be treated
as an equal and to speak for itself.
Mr. President, there are moments in the
life of a nation when its people are
called to remember who they have always
been.
This is such a moment for us. And so I
begin with something deeply personal to
my people and my country and that is our
name.
For many years the world has known our
country as Noru.
Noru is how our name sounded to those
who found it hard to say and the world
kept it. But it is not the name our
people used among themselves.
I rise on my first point not to announce
a change but to affirm a truth.
Long before our country took its place
among the family of nations,
long before our name appeared on
international records,
our people knew our homeland by one
name, Na.
That name carries the memory of our
ancestors, our language, and our
identity. It has been there all along,
never lost, never absent. Today, we
restore NATO. We do not make this choice
to erase our past. We make it because we
honor it. We do so with respect for our
history and with gratitude for the
journey. NorU has carried us through to
our independence and our place on the
international stage. Mr. President,
my government's priority is investing in
our people and our future generations.
Restoring our name gives back to them a
piece of the inheritance because the
identity handed down by our own
ancestors has a place in the community
of nations.
Because their history and language
matter because they too have the right
to inherit a nation that knows itself,
names itself and speaks of itself.
In light of this year's theme, let me
say this. There can be no genuine trust
and no true transformation without
respect for the identity, history,
language and rights of every people to
be treated as an equal and to speak for
itself.
I take the opportunity now to convey my
sincerest gratitude to the secretariat
and to this assembly and the many
institutions and partners who have taken
steps to recognize our restored name. It
may seem a small courtesy but it means a
great deal at home. And so, Mr.
President, I say this with the greatest
pride.
That means I am from NATO and so is
every person I have the honor to speak
for today. We take our seats under that
name. Proud of where we have come from.
Confident in who we are and determined
to carry our name into the future. What
I ask of the world costs nothing.
Join us in recognizing and respecting
the identity that is already ours. Say
our name.
Mr. President,
Narrow is an ocean state. We are not
merely guardians of the ocean, but
rightful participants in its future. For
Narrow, the ocean represents both
opportunity and responsibility.
Never one without the other.
Both are essential.
or the United Nations Convention on the
Law of the Sea is left hollow.
Today I focus on a part of it that
belongs to no one, the deep seabed area
beyond national jurisdiction. Mr.
President, the convention established
the international seabed authority and
charged it with a clear legal obligation
to put in place regulations and regulate
activities in parallel with sponsoring
states.
Its role is not to determine whether
deep sea bed mining is as a matter of
policy public policy a correct course of
action. NA joined trusting in the
commitment set out in the convention and
the 1994 agreement.
For 15 years
NA invested critical resources in
sponsoring the exploration of a portion
of the deep seabed. Our sponsored entity
Nori on Nor ocean resources
has contributed about one pabyte of data
more than onethird of all claren
kibbitanzone data held in the
authorities's deep data.
We called on the authority to seek an
advisory opinion on the responsibilities
of sponsoring states and we followed it.
We established a national regulator with
the powers and due diligence obligations
that opinion requires.
At every stage, our decisions have
rested on the best available scientific
evidence on the convention and on that
opinion. At every stage, we have called
for the mining code to be finished. And
when progress stalled, we looked to the
1994 agreement and invoked the 2-year
rule. We were told then that we were
rushing. That was 5 years ago and today
the rules remain unwritten.
We are participating in the first
contentious proceedings before the
seabed disputes chamber because our
obligations as a sponsoring state
require legal clarity.
For 15 years we have done everything a
member state can do consistent with our
obligations as a sponsoring state and
today we continue to wait.
Mr. President, there's a general
understanding within the authorities
council that nothing is agreed until
everything is agreed and that the
regulations will be adopted by
consensus.
Achieving that is a great challenge for
an institution whose members remain
deeply divided on whether deep seabed
mining should proceed at all.
a question the convention never asked
the authority to decide.
NATO welcomes every effort to ensure
that seabed mineral development proceeds
responsibly.
And I ask this assembly to reckon with
this. A principle declared in 1970
and a bargain struck in 1994.
Both in this hall still wait for the
rules that would give them effect.
When a multilateral process cannot
deliver, the world does not stand still.
Those with the means to act will not
wait. And every year of delay makes that
more likely not less. That is why the
theme of this session matters. A
multilateral system that cannot deliver
for a state like mine does not deliver
at all.
That holds here in this assembly and in
any institution we build. NATO therefore
calls upon the authority.
Let the waiting end adopt the rules.
Similarly, Mr. President, a multilateral
agency with which we see of increasing
irrelevance
to the NATO, namely the International
Criminal Court is one which calls for
NATO to end its participation and to
revoke its membership.
Before I depart New York, NATO will be
depositing our instruments of withdrawal
with the Rome Statute Repository.
Mr. President, my government's central
purpose is to put NATO on its own feet.
That work is underway.
Our trust fund to which we contribute
more than 10% of our revenue every
single year so that NATO has something
to stand on
when and if these arrangements end. Our
fisheries, the seabed joining the
Eggmons group. New revenue through our
investment and residence programs.
A virtual asset regulator built with
full due diligence obligations before
the industry regulates.
Our valuable, our valuable partnerships,
and behind all of it, investment in
health, education, and sport so that our
people are not only better off, but
healthier and better prepared.
We are building an economy that not that
does not depend on any single
arrangement. And by every measure of
fiscal discipline, we have done what was
asked of us. Yet the measure by which we
are assessed sees none of it. It sees
income and it sees nothing else. It does
not capture the full story of my nation,
the true cost of our geographic
isolation,
the fragility of our limited economic
base, or the devastating impact a single
disaster can have on our people and our
progress. In January 2027,
NATO will be considered a high income
country in the OECD system.
That does reflect real progress.
But progress should not be punished
because 58% of our revenue comes from
bilateral arrangements that are not ours
to renew.
87% of the food our people eat is
purchased and imported. We have one
runway, one port, one road that connects
everywhere.
None of that appears in how we are
assessed. That is why we strongly
support the multi-dimensional
vulnerability index or MVI and the
United Nations efforts to pilot the
tool. Its full implementation is
essential to ensuring that countries
like ours are fairly assessed and
adequately supported. It requires it
recognizes that vulnerability is complex
and it must be seen, measured and acted
upon. Mr. President, we acknowledge the
significant process progress made by
some development partners and financial
institutions in adopting vulnerability
assessments and reviewing the
eligibility criteria. The Asian
Development Bank ADB weighs
vulnerability alongside income and its
own policy names my nation as the
clearest example of why income alone
conceals what small island states face.
As a country that is ranked the fifth
most vulnerable country in the world on
the index and the most vulnerable in the
Pacific, we welcome these developments
as positive steps.
But the gap remains. Not all have taken
the necessary steps to truly recognize
our realities. I therefore urge all who
have yet to do so, including the World
Bank, to weigh vulnerability alongside
income in decisions on eligibility as
the ADB already does. If the
international community is truly serious
about restoring trust and managing
transformation,
it must demonstrate that commitment
where it matters most with those who are
most vulnerable.
Mr. President, I turn to my final point.
No country of our size stands alone.
NATO is a friend to all and an enemy to
none.
NATO's partnerships are not all of one
kind.
Some are born of kinship, some of shared
interests. Some have been built through
decades of cooperation, and some are
grounded in the conviction that when a
wrong persists, it must be named and
addressed.
Each relationship matters. None is a
substitute for another and none comes at
the expense of another.
Mr. Present small states are
increasingly asked to choose between
partners, between blocks, between
competing visions of the world.
NATO would not be made to choose. We
will work with every partner who
respects our sovereignty and our right
to decide our own future.
That is not neutrality.
It is called independence.
Partnership does not mean agreement on
everything. It means standing together
where interests align and standing on
principle where they do not.
A friend I speak for today has been
waiting for justice. I am asking this
assembly to honor its word and I cannot
then fall silent when that word is
broken for someone else. For 33
consecutive years, this assembly has
called for an end to the embargo against
Cuba.
NATO reiterates
that call and we encourage dialogue
grounded in full respect for sovereignty
because sovereign equality must be more
than a principle written in the charter.
Whatever this assembly intends to
deliver, it will be delivered through
partnership and cooperation or not at
all.
So I extend an invitation to the members
of this assembly.
Invest in our people. Invest in our
economy that rests on more than a
handful of arrangements. Invest in
institutions that will outlast my
government and the next. Invest in the
infrastructure, connectivity and
opportunities that distance has too
often denied us. What NATO offers this
assembly is not dependence but
participation.
Not expectation but contribution.
Not a not a beneficiary but a partner.
Invest with us not simply in us. Mr.
president I've raised today concerns
this organization and what it has
promised. So does this.
The security council does not reflect
the world as it is. It reflects the
world as it was in 1945 when most of the
countries in this hall did not yet exist
as sovereign states.
NATO therefore calls for a reform that
expands both the permanent and
non-permanent categories.
A body that speaks for all of us should
look like all of us.
Mr. President, as I draw my statement to
a close, the matters I have raised may
appear separate. They are not. Our name
is about sovereignty.
How we are measured is about justice.
The deep seabed is about opportunity and
responsibility.
Our partnerships are about standing as
equals.
One principle binds them. the right of
every people to be treated as an equal
and to speak for itself.
You have convened this assembly to
restore trust, to manage transformation
and to deliver for all. Trust is
restored when promises are kept.
Transformation is managed when decisions
lead to action.
And we deliver for all only when you
deliver for the small.
Everything NATO has asked for today was
agreed in this hall long before I took
this floor. I am not asking this
assembly to be braver than it has ever
been. I am challenging you to be as good
as your word.
Say our name.
Let the waiting end.
Let vulnerability be measured honestly
and treat us as partners. May God bless
the Republic of NATO. May God bless the
United Nations. Mate, I thank you.
On behalf of the assembly, I wish to
thank the president and head of state of
the republic of Nairo.
